title: Possibility
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes trusting one's inner power and inherent wholeness, rather than relying on external sources or specific outcomes. By letting go of conceptual thinking and embracing silence, we can tap into our true nature and live authentically, without attachment to particular hopes or expectations. This approach encourages us to cultivate openness and receptivity, allowing life to unfold naturally and manifesting hope in small yet meaningful ways, such as kindness towards ourselves and others.

sentences.text: Well, good evening, everyone.
Spring's finally come to Bellingham.
Isn't it wonderful to see the sun out and the sunset this evening?
Thank you for coming.
This talk has been taking a while to gel, and I realized I was thinking, what am I going to call this thing?
I had a bunch of different titles and nothing seemed to fit right.
And I was driving over here, I said, oh, it's about possibility.
This talk is about possibility.
Maybe something like the ground or the sound of possibility.
I usually pull my talks out of something that's been stirring in me in my day-to-day life.
I had been noticing how irritable and overwhelmed I've felt at times in these last many weeks.
One of my friends commented recently about the density of her own life, and that's how my life has felt.
It's felt very dense, both in personal events and also in the events in the world and around us.
So I've been thinking about how to respond, how to find my ground in the midst of that.
A few weeks ago, a poem came across on Facebook, which I spent a little bit of time on.
It's a poem by a poet named Jane Hirschfeld, who some of you might know, and maybe some of you saw that poem.
It's not published.
She wrote it not long ago and sent it out as an offering, asking that people not share it, but to cut and paste it or to pass it on personally.
So I'm passing on this poem of hers.

Not long thereafter, I also heard a talk or a conversation that happened at Upaia Zen Center at the beginning of the chaplaincy program there between a good Dharma brother and teacher of mine, Hosean Alan Sinaki, and one of the contemporary thinkers who's well thought of these days, Rebecca Solnit, whose work some of you may know.
It was a lovely talk that they entitled Hope and Hopelessness.
So I've borrowed somewhat from that talk, and I am starting with Jane's poem because it really touched something very deep in me.
I've been sitting with it and examining, without examining, if you know what I mean, why that is.
It's called On the Fifth Day.
The fifth day in biblical terms is the day the birds and ocean and animals were created.
It's also Friday, named for the goddess of fertility and love.
It's Venus's day.
It's also, if you're a Lord of the Rings fan, the day Gandalf was due back after leaving in the midst of the big assault that was about to happen.
He was due back on the fifth day.
The fifth lunar day is also represented by a unicorn.
He calls for fighting for your opinion and principles, or protecting unjustly convicted people, or for unfolding your feelings.
And in Kwanzaa, which you may know is a relatively recent holiday celebrated in African-American communities, the fifth day is Naya, the day of renewing our purpose for living.
I have no idea which one Jane Hirschfeld has in mind.
Can you hear me okay?
No?
Really?
Do you want to pull your chair up close?
If anyone else needs to move around and come closer too, please do so.
I don't know which one she has in mind, but I went through all of this just now because I find all of them relevant in some way to this poem.
So settle into zazen mind and just receive this enormous gift.
*On the fifth day, the scientists who studied the rivers were forbidden to speak or to study the rivers.
The scientists who studied the air were told not to speak of the air and the ones who worked for the farmers were silenced and the ones who worked for the bees.
Someone from deep in the badlands began posting facts.
The facts were told not to speak and were taken away.
The facts surprised to be taken were silent.
Now it was only the rivers that spoke of the rivers and only the wind that spoke of its bees.
While the unpausing factual buds of the fruit trees continued to move toward their fruit, the silence spoke loudly of silence and the rivers kept speaking of rivers, of boulders and air.
In gravity and silence, the untreated, untested rivers kept speaking.
Bus drivers, shelf stalkers, code writers, machinists, accountants, lab techs, cellists kept speaking.
They spoke the fifth day of silence.*
I've read this many times and it still touches me very deeply.
There are so many sentiments in here, but somehow to me it speaks of hope.
Hope, by definition, is a feeling of expectation and a desire for a certain thing to happen.
Wanting something to happen.
Or it refers to a person or a thing that may help or save someone.
Isn't that interesting?
Rivers and buds saving something.
Usually when we talk about hope we speak about something specific we want.
Usually we want it for ourselves.
It's a personal thing, or maybe even if we want it, like peace for the world.
When I was in ninth grade my geometry teacher went around and asked everyone what they hoped for, and I was the only one in the world that said peace with the Russians.
Everyone else wanted something for Christmas.
But usually it's something we want for ourselves or someone we know.
Maybe it's a wish for our own peace of mind.
Usually it's a hope that we request.
We think we're requesting of something larger.
We put it out to the universe or we ask God or we ask Buddha.
There's some power larger than our life.
This kind of hope is mundane.
It's what we sometimes refer to as ordinary hope.
There's nothing wrong with it.
There's a certain kind of hope.
We'd say it's not really Buddhist, though.
I like to churn things up a little bit when I give talks, so I challenge you a little bit.
It's not really Buddhist to have this kind of hope, maybe.
Usually we say we sit facing the white wall and let go of thoughts, having no expectation of getting anything.
That's what we normally think.
We have no design even on becoming a Buddha.
No design on being enlightened.
We just sit.
That's really our zazen.
Usually our hope is about appealing to something beyond ourselves.
Something that comes from outside.
Maybe it's good luck.
Maybe it's a fortunate serendipity.
Maybe it's the right circumstances we want.
But actually the ground of our practice is something that comes from inside.
Suzuki Roshi calls it our inner power.
He says, stand up by the ground.
He suggests, in a beautiful little talk in Not Always So, that we're protected from the inside.
We're protected from the inside so we don't expect any help from the outside, is what he says.
What we might say instead in this practice is that we trust in the inherent wholeness of our lives.
What is that?
How do we know that?
We talk about our inner aspiration or vow.
It's really our Bodhi mind.
So we actually let go of hope.
Or we let go really of clinging to the idea of hope, of knowing what it is that we're hoping for.
We're not looking for something specific.
We're manifesting our aspiration or our vow.
Katagiri calls this keeping it warm in our heart for a while.
Allowing it to incubate.
The buds go on unbutting themselves in the spring.
Sometimes we talk about this as not knowing being most intimate.
But I actually think, it's a wonderful story if you know that koan, but I actually think it's kind of too heady for this.
It's a kind of encouragement to trust not knowing.
But the kind of intimacy, the kind of holding open in your heart for a while, is the way the birds are just the birds, and the animals and the plants tell us how to do it in another way.
My first teacher showed me too.
My first teacher was involved in sitting, among many things that she did.
She was involved in sitting at the tracks out in Livermore, which is about an hour and a half drive from Berkeley when there's traffic.
Every week on Fridays at a given time, there would be a train that would go by carrying nuclear waste.
A group of people would go and sit zazen at the tracks and bear witness to it.
One day, one of the members of the community came up to her and said, do you really think that makes any difference, to do that?
And she said, I don't know.
But it's most important that I do it.
It's most important that she follow her inner voice to manifest in this time, in that moment, in that way.
The plants don't question if they should grow and the birds don't question if they should breathe.
They don't say, is there climate change?
Will there be enough food?
Is it too hot?
Is it too cold?
They just do.
That's what's asked of us in this practice, too.
That's what Jane Hirschfeld is pointing to.
We have our own inner compass.
We might think of it as vow.
That's very useful.
Many of us have been inspired by my teacher Shohaku Okumura's book, Living by Vow.
I say that because I respect him enormously.
We conceptualize it in that way, and it's very useful.
We will say our Bodhisattva vows at the end of this evening.
I think that helps to ask what matters the most to me and how I live my life.
But in a way, it's conceptual.
In reality, we manifest our vows in our daily life.
We manifest them in our everyday activity, with what we're doing.
We manifest them by living them, by putting them in action now and now and now.
Our vows are like when we live our lives like weeds grow.
We just are who we are.
The birds return, the bulbs peek up, and the wind blows.
When we are in tune with our true nature and know our proper place in the world, we're like that, too.
If we're in harmony with ourselves and our world, then our vow naturally manifests.
We act in the world because that's what there is to do.
We don't think equations and outcomes.
We don't even think really about whether we're getting the outcome that we wanted.
Well, we do, but not really so much, if you know what I mean.
You can quibble with this.
We can have a conversation, but I think you know what I'm pointing at.
We don't hold back or change course because we aren't sure what we want for our own personal lives won't happen.
When we're really in the groove of our lives, we just do it.
Vow isn't something we take or do.
It is born in us.
It is alive in us.
It manifests us in the way a tree grows from an acorn.
How do we know it?
It comes in silence, doesn't it?
That's why we sit zazen.
This is what occurs in zazen.
We return to the sound of no sound, to the silence greater than our own mind.

Those of us who've sat for a while, even if you've sat one period and had that experience of having the quiet and the silence of your mind, you understand on some level that your life is part of a fabric of something bigger.
Somehow you know something deeper.
I can't really put it into words without spoiling it.
The silence, this is greater than the scientists' studies or the facts or the facts that were quiet.
The silence of our own inner self, a Dharma sister posted recently, "Listening to the land around me, learning: the apricots are first to blossom."
Martin Luther King famously said the long arc of the moral universe bends towards justice.
I'd say maybe, or maybe not.
I think it's more like a pendulum.
But I do want to say things don't look like what we think.
We think something is a certain way, but we don't really know.
Probably some of you have heard the story about the Tibetan farmer and his luck.
Do you know this story?
The Tibetan farmer's horse runs away, right?
People come to him and say, "Oh, bad luck, bad luck."
And he says, "Maybe."
The next day his horse comes running back with two more.
People come to him and say, "Oh, good luck, good luck."
And he says, "Maybe."
A few days later his son is riding the horse and one of the wild horses bucks him off and breaks his leg.
People in the town come to him and say, "Oh, bad luck."
"Maybe."
Two days later a war breaks out and all the young men in town are conscripted, except for the farmer's son.
Good luck?
Maybe.
We don't know.
Rebecca Solnick gave a wonderful example for those of you who are as old as I am or remember.
The Clam Shell Alliance began in 1975, and it was the first time people organized politically as a group against nuclear waste.
They conducted many nonviolent demonstrations.
There were over 1,400 of them arrested at one point, and they failed.
Nuclear plants went on.
But did they?
Their organizing tactics are actually what's being used around the world today for grassroots organizing.
Did they succeed?
Did they fail?
The facts were released from the badlands.
I don't know about you, but I was profoundly moved by the prayerful vigilance that the Native people held in Standing Rock.

Whether you're pro-oil or not, that people would represent their rights by praying under all conditions, peacefully and nonviolently, under all circumstances, was a great inspiration of having a voice to say what matters deeply.
This is my vow.
This is how my life manifests.
This is what's most important.
The pipeline's being finished.
Did they succeed?
Did they fail?
I don't know.
So as Buddhists we understand the effects are most often indirect, and that karmic activity is so subtle and intertwined that we can't know its effect.
That's why the Buddha refused to explain it.

But what we do know is that we have a karmic impact, and that hope, I think, can also be paired with a sense of responsibility: a responsibility to live our life and live out our true being and what we're really called for.
There's a second dictionary definition of hope, and that is a feeling of trust.
In Buddhism our practice asks us to trust ourselves.
Be a lamp unto yourself.
Trust what you're called to manifest in this life and do that.
That's your responsibility.
Response: the bodhisattva's response to this moment, what needs to be done now.
Ability: that's you manifesting your life.
Sometimes we dedicate the merit of our chanting.
We say, may the two wheels, the material and the spiritual wheel of this temple, go smoothly, and may calamities not befall our people, country or benefactors.
But we're not asking for help.
The spirit of it is different.

We're asking to be responsible, to conduct ourselves with perfect calmness and with the conviction of our practice, to manifest our lives like the unpausing factual buds of the fruit trees continuing to move toward their fruit, like bus drivers, shelf stalkers, code riders, machinists, accountants, lab techs, cellists.
If I knew each of you I'd go around the room and say what you're going to do tomorrow, one by one.
Thank you.
I don't know if there's time, oh, if there's time for a couple of questions.
If anyone has anything they want to say, or a response, or what comes up for you, or what you're going to do tomorrow.
**Participant:** Would it be possible to post a copy of that poem on a bulletin board, or would that be outside the spirit of what the poem was offering?
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** I think as long as you don't copy it down and send it out to people, I think that's fine.
Maybe I'll read it again.
*On the fifth day, on the fifth day the scientists who studied the rivers were forbidden to speak or to study the rivers.
The scientists who studied the air were told not to speak of the air, and the ones who worked for the farmers were silenced, and the ones who worked for the bees.
Someone from deep in the badlands began posting facts.
The facts were told not to speak and were taken away.
The facts surprised to be taken were silent.
Now it was only the rivers that spoke of the rivers and only the wind that spoke of its bees, while the unpausing factual buds of the fruit trees continued to move toward their fruit.
The silence spoke loudly of silence and the rivers kept speaking of rivers, of boulder, of air.
In gravity and silence the untreated, untested rivers kept speaking.
Bus drivers, shell stalkers, code riders, machinists, accountants, lab techs, cellists kept speaking.
They spoke the fifth day of silence.*
What's your experience of this?
What's been your experience in these last weeks and months?
No matter what exactly we think of what's happening, we can't help but be affected by it.
The dog tells me that he still loves me.
What you said about noticing that you had been, I don't remember the words you used, but that you felt this underlying sense in yourself?
**Participant:** Anxiety, irritability.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** There you go.

**Participant:** So my husband and I noticed that we had been squabbling a lot more, and then we remembered how years ago we went on a date to see the movie W, and when we got out of the movie we had the biggest fight of our entire life.
And we realized with both of those things that we weren't fighting with each other about each other.
We were picking up the energy.
I appreciate hearing that come from you, because I think that we all can, like Tink said tonight to me, give ourselves a break and say, okay, this is it.
This is what's happening.
We're still here.
Our buds are still getting ready to bloom, and we are going to keep living for a while.
I think it's really important in these times to be very kind to yourself and very kind to each other.
Everyone needs extra kindness.
It's the antidote to the tenor and pitch of conversation that's around.
And if we can hold kindness here and recognize everyone needs it, we can help create that.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Yeah.
Yeah, thank you.
**Participant:** What you just said makes me think about just how amazingly infectious positive or negative emotion is.
It's really powerful.
So it's hard for us to remember, because we feel so separate, right, that how we choose to be is affecting so many people.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Oh, Ken.
**Participant:** This is exactly appropriate at this moment, but one month from the day the silence will, the facts will break for silence, and there's a march in Seattle for science.
And I personally am going to be down, being rather loud for the facts, and I'm happy to give at least three other people a ride if they wish to come.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** So we'll be driving in the science car.
**Participant:** No.
No.
See me if you wish to go to the March for Science in Seattle.
The car's almost silent.
The car is silent.
I'm sorry.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** So it's April 22nd in Seattle.
Earth Day.
**Participant:** Yes, on Earth Day.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Thank you, Ken.
Anyone else?
**Participant:** I have a little reflection.
I was listening to the confirmation hearings for Gorsuch.
And recently, I've been really disturbed by what's going on, as many people have been, getting myself caught up in it.
And as I was listening today, it's different than reading the news, because I was hearing their voices, and I could hear, he sounds like a sincere kind of a guy, in his position.
And then I was listening to both sides interview him, and they just sounded like people.
And hearing their voices changed my perspective a bit.
And then the other feeling I got was they're just words, and that it was a theater, more of a theater.
And it really lightened me up in a sense.
I didn't feel so reactive.
Just hearing them as people, I guess.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** It is true.
There's a difference between the person and the actions.
Yes, you can see the person as a person.
You can understand the circumstances that bring forth that person in that moment.
And then there's actually what they're doing or going to do.
And those are important distinctions.
Anyone else [unclear: "before we tell us"]?
**Participant:** This question arises: does hope carry responsibility?
Or is it harmful to think so?
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Our lives carry responsibility.
Our lives as Buddhist practitioners carry a responsibility to manifest themselves.
The bird has a responsibility to be a bird.
The buds have a responsibility to flowers above.
We have a responsibility to live our lives, and because we're practitioners, to follow the precepts.
There's a certain morality or ethic about how we live our lives, and we have a responsibility to examine that for ourselves and to manifest it in whatever way.
So that's how I'd answer your question.
**Participant:** I have a hope for the birds.
And I feel a responsibility around that hope.
And I've watched birds and studied birds on trips to search for birds, and I love birds.
And we have the Anna's hummingbird up here in the northwest, who has come to winter up here.
And they've shown through research that the bird has really begun to evolve and adapt in response to climate change over the years.
And so this winter was a very harsh winter for the birds, and a number of them died.
But I fed them, and I fed them all winter, and I had a little practice: every morning I would put a fresh feeder out and I would watch it, and if it froze I put another one out.
And I've done this for the last few months.
And yesterday one of the Rufus hummingbirds that typically migrate arrived at one of the feeders.
And so I have a hope for the birds, and tomorrow I'm going to feed them again.
And I feel like it is a responsibility that I really truly embrace as a small, or slash, or who knows how significant a practice it is.
But we have a visitor from another state who asked me today, and he said, well, do you think there's any difference?
So I was very timid when you said that.
And I said, you know, I don't know.
But it's something that I feel I have to do.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Bernadette is manifesting Bernadette.
Thank you.
